lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting ready: your documents and your benefits list
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Gather the documents VA asks for and list the benefits you may apply for.
This lesson builds toward: Before you apply for any VA benefit, you will gather the documents VA asks for, starting with your DD214, and list the benefits you may apply for, with missing documents marked and copies kept in a safe place.
VA benefits are things you earned through your service. Common ones include disability compensation (monthly payments for conditions caused or made worse by service), VA health care, education benefits such as the GI Bill, and Veteran Readiness and Employment. There are others, such as home loan help, pension and burial benefits. Each has its own rules.
The most important paper is your DD214 or other separation documents. VA uses it to confirm your service. Keep copies in a safe place. If you cannot find yours, va.gov explains how to request your military records.
Other things VA may ask for: your Social Security number, bank details for direct deposit, your medical records and the names of your doctors, information about your spouse and dependents, insurance cards, and your income from last year for some health care decisions.
Make a sign-in account on va.gov so you can apply online, upload documents and check status. Use the official site only. Do not share your sign-in with anyone, and never type your Social Security number or medical details into an AI chatbot.
Step by step:
- Find your DD214 or other separation papers and make copies.
- Gather medical records and a list of your doctors.
- Write down which benefits you want to look at: disability, health care, education, others.
- Create a sign-in account on va.gov.
- Keep everything in one folder.
Words to know:
- DD214: the document that shows your military service and how you separated.
- Disability compensation: monthly, tax-free payments for conditions caused or made worse by military service.
- Dependent: a spouse, child or other family member who relies on you.
Official sources:
- VA: How to file a VA disability claim
Try it now: Make a folder (paper or a secure folder on your own computer) and put in it, or list what is missing: your DD214, medical records, a list of your doctors and your dependents' details. Write down the benefits you want to look at.
You can now gather the documents VA asks for and list the benefits you may apply for.

check.q: Why keep copies of your DD214 in a safe place?
options: So you can post it online
So an AI can read it
VA uses it to confirm your service, and you will need it again
check.why: Your DD214 confirms your service for many benefits, so keep copies safe.

check.q: You want an AI chatbot to help you understand your benefits. What do you leave out?
options: Your Social Security number and medical details
check.why: Private numbers and medical details never go into an AI chatbot.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Filing a disability compensation claim
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose how you will file a disability claim and protect your start date.
This lesson builds toward: For conditions you think are connected to your service, you will choose how you will file a disability claim and list evidence for each condition, using an official way to file and protecting your start date.
You can file a disability claim online on va.gov, by mail using VA Form 21-526EZ, in person at a VA regional office, or with help from an accredited representative. VA says that starting the online form sets your effective date automatically.
Your effective date matters because it can decide when payments start counting from. If you start online, VA will use the date you started as your date of claim as long as you finish within 365 days. If you file on paper, you can submit an intent to file first to hold a possible effective date while you gather evidence.
Evidence makes or breaks a claim. VA reviews your DD214 or separation papers and your service treatment records. Add what you have: private doctor records, and statements from you or people who saw how the condition affects you. List every condition you believe is connected to your service.
After you file, VA may schedule an exam. Go to it. Check your claim status on va.gov. VA publishes its average processing time, which changes, so check va.gov for the current number. If you disagree with a decision, there are ways to ask for a review; an accredited representative can help.
Step by step:
- Decide how to file: online, by mail (VA Form 21-526EZ), in person, or with an accredited representative.
- If filing online, start the form to set your date, and finish within 365 days.
- If filing on paper, think about submitting an intent to file first.
- List every condition and gather your evidence.
- Go to any VA exam and check your status on va.gov.
Words to know:
- Effective date: the date VA uses to decide when your benefit payments start counting from.
- Intent to file: a notice to VA that you plan to file, which can hold your effective date while you gather evidence.
- Evidence: records and statements that support your claim.
- Service connection: a link between a health condition and your military service.
Official sources:
- VA: How to file a VA disability claim
Try it now: Write down every health condition you think may be connected to your service. Next to each, write one piece of evidence you have or could get. Then decide which way you will file and write it at the top.
You can now choose how to file a disability claim, protect your effective date and gather evidence for each condition.

check.q: Which is an official way to file a disability claim?
options: Texting a stranger who offers help
Posting in a social media group
Emailing a company that charges a percentage
check.why: Filing online at va.gov is one of VA's official ways to file.

check.q: You listed a knee condition from service. What do you write next to it?
options: One piece of evidence, such as service treatment or doctor records
check.why: Each condition needs evidence, such as service treatment or doctor records.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Applying for VA health care
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Apply for VA health care with the right information ready.
This lesson builds toward: Using a practice checklist, you will prepare the information for a VA health care application (10-10EZ) and choose how you will apply, with your service history, exposures, insurance and income marked as ready or still needed.
VA health care is a separate application from disability compensation. You apply with VA Form 10-10EZ, the Application for Health Benefits.
You can apply online on va.gov, by phone through the VA health benefits hotline at 877-222-8387 (VA lists it as Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Eastern time), by mail, or in person at a VA medical center or clinic. An accredited representative can also help.
Have ready: your DD214 and service history, including any toxic or hazardous exposures; Social Security numbers for you, your spouse and qualified dependents; your insurance cards, including Medicare or a job plan; and your household income from last year. VA says you may leave income out, but it may need it to decide your application.
Example: a Marine who served overseas has asthma and wants a primary care doctor. He applies online for health care the same week he files his disability claim, lists his exposure history, and books his first appointment once he is enrolled.
Step by step:
- Gather your DD214, exposure history, Social Security numbers and insurance cards.
- Write down last year's household income.
- Apply online at va.gov, by phone at 877-222-8387, by mail, or in person.
- Watch for VA's decision and book your first appointment.
Words to know:
- VA Form 10-10EZ: the application for VA health benefits.
- Toxic exposure: contact during service with harmful things like burn pits, chemicals or radiation.
Official sources:
- VA: How to apply for VA health care
Try it now: Fill in a practice checklist for the 10-10EZ: DD214 (have it or not), exposure history, insurance cards, last year's household income. Mark what you have and what you still need, and choose how you will apply.
You can now apply for VA health care with the right information and know the ways to apply.

check.why: The 10-10EZ is the application for VA health care.

check.q: You are filling in your health care checklist. What do you include about your service?
options: Your service history, including any toxic or hazardous exposures
check.why: VA asks about your service history and exposures when you apply for health care.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: The GI Bill and free help

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Understanding the GI Bill
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main GI Bill programs and list what they can pay for.
This lesson builds toward: Given your career goal, you will describe the main GI Bill programs and two kinds of training they could pay for, naming training that fits your goal.
The GI Bill helps pay for school and training. The main program today is the Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33), for people who served on active duty after September 10, 2001. It can help pay for school and cover costs while you train for a job.
Other programs include the Montgomery GI Bill Active Duty (Chapter 30) and the Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserve (Chapter 1606) for members of the Reserve and National Guard. Which one you can use depends on your service.
The GI Bill is not only for four-year college. VA lists uses such as undergraduate and graduate degrees, non-college degree programs, on-the-job training and apprenticeships, licensing and certification tests, flight training, online learning and more. The Yellow Ribbon Program can help cover tuition the Post-9/11 GI Bill does not, at schools that take part.
Some service members can transfer unused Post-9/11 benefits to a spouse or children. If you already have Post-9/11 benefits, check how much you have left on your GI Bill Statement of Benefits on va.gov.
Words to know:
- GI Bill: VA education benefits that help pay for school or training.
- Post-9/11 GI Bill: the GI Bill for people who served on active duty after September 10, 2001 (Chapter 33).
- Yellow Ribbon Program: a program that can cover tuition the Post-9/11 GI Bill does not, at schools that take part.
- Apprenticeship: paid on-the-job training for a skilled trade.
Official sources:
- VA: About GI Bill benefits
Try it now: Write down the career you want. Then write two kinds of GI Bill-eligible training that could get you there, for example an electrician apprenticeship and a certificate program, or a degree and a licensing test.
You can now name the main GI Bill programs and match GI Bill-eligible training to a career goal.

check.q: What is the Post-9/11 GI Bill also called?
check.why: The Post-9/11 GI Bill is Chapter 33.

check.q: You want to become an electrician without a four-year degree. What do you write in your plan?
options: The GI Bill only pays for degrees
Give up on the GI Bill
An apprenticeship or on-the-job training the GI Bill can help with
check.why: The GI Bill can help with apprenticeships and on-the-job training, not only degrees.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Applying for the GI Bill and choosing a school
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Apply for education benefits and compare schools before you enroll.
This lesson builds toward: Given two schools or training programs, you will compare them in the GI Bill Comparison Tool and plan your education benefit application, with two facts about each and your application checked before you submit.
Apply for education benefits online at va.gov. If you apply by mail, use VA Form 22-1990, the Application for VA Education Benefits, for the Post-9/11 GI Bill and the Montgomery GI Bill programs. Family members using transferred benefits use a different form, VA Form 22-1990e.
Have ready: your Social Security number, bank details for direct deposit, your education and military history, and basic details about the school or training program. VA says you cannot change the application after you submit it, so check it first.
VA says it takes about 30 days on average to process education claims, but check va.gov for current times. When you are approved, VA sends a Certificate of Eligibility. Give a copy to your school's certifying official, often found in the veterans or military services office.
Before you enroll, compare schools with VA's GI Bill Comparison Tool on va.gov, and ask the school about costs, job results and whether it takes part in Yellow Ribbon. Be careful of schools that pressure you to sign up fast.
Step by step:
- Choose your program and school or training.
- Compare it with the GI Bill Comparison Tool on va.gov.
- Gather your Social Security number, bank details, education and military history.
- Apply online, or by mail with VA Form 22-1990.
- Give your Certificate of Eligibility to the school's certifying official.
Words to know:
- Certificate of Eligibility (COE): VA's letter that shows which education benefit you have and how much.
- School certifying official: the person at a school who tells VA you are enrolled.
- VA Form 22-1990: the Application for VA Education Benefits.
Official sources:
- VA: How to apply for the GI Bill and related benefits
- VA: GI Bill Comparison Tool
Try it now: Pick two schools or training programs for your career goal. Look each one up in the GI Bill Comparison Tool on va.gov, and write down two facts about each and one question you would ask its veterans office.
You can now apply for GI Bill benefits, compare schools before enrolling and use your Certificate of Eligibility.

check.q: What does the GI Bill Comparison Tool help you do?
options: Compare schools and training programs before you enroll
Change your GI Bill after you submit
check.why: The Comparison Tool shows facts about schools and programs so you can compare them.

check.q: You finished your GI Bill application. What do you do before you submit?
options: Check it carefully, because you cannot change it after you submit
Submit it fast and fix it later
Ask a stranger to submit it
check.why: You cannot change the application after you submit it, so check it first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting free help, and avoiding people who charge to file
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a free, VA-accredited representative and spot people who should not be paid.
This lesson builds toward: When you want help with a claim, you will find a free VA-accredited representative and identify the warning signs of someone who should not be paid, with a representative's name and contact and three warning signs written down.
You do not have to file alone. VA accredits three kinds of representatives: Veterans Service Organization (VSO) representatives, attorneys and claims agents. VA says the services of an accredited VSO representative on your claim are always free. They can help gather evidence, file a claim, ask for a decision review and talk with VA for you. Many states and counties also have veterans service officers.
Find one with VA's tool, "Find a VA-accredited representative or VSO", on va.gov. VA says to make sure anyone helping with your claim is accredited before you choose them.
Attorneys and claims agents may charge fees, but VA says only after VA has decided your initial claim, and only with a signed fee agreement. That means anyone who charges you to file your first claim, or promises a higher rating for a fee, is a warning sign. Some unaccredited people, sometimes called "claim sharks", ask for a share of your future back pay, sign-in details or upfront fees.
Never give anyone your va.gov sign-in. If you believe a representative acted wrongly or charged an unfair fee, you can contact VA's Office of General Counsel, and you must act quickly on fee disputes.
Step by step:
- Open VA's "Find a VA-accredited representative or VSO" tool on va.gov.
- Search near you and choose a VSO representative (free).
- Confirm they are accredited before you share anything.
- Never pay to file an initial claim, and never share your va.gov sign-in.
- Report problems to VA's Office of General Counsel.
Words to know:
- VSO: Veterans Service Organization: a group whose accredited representatives help veterans with claims for free.
- Accredited: approved by VA to help with VA claims.
- Claim shark: an unaccredited person or company that charges veterans to file claims.
Official sources:
- VA: Accredited representative FAQs
- VA: Find a VA-accredited representative or VSO
Try it now: Final task: use VA's "Find a VA-accredited representative or VSO" tool to find one free representative near you and write down their name and how to reach them. Then finish your VA benefits action plan with your document checklist, the benefits you will apply for and how, your GI Bill plan if you have one, and three warning signs of claim sharks. Take the first step on one benefit.
You can now find a free, accredited VSO, spot people who should not be paid to file, and start your VA benefits action plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Document checklist No checklist, or the DD214 is not on it. A checklist starting with the DD214, with missing documents marked. Notes where each document is kept and how to get any that are missing. Benefits and how to apply Benefits are listed without how to apply. Each benefit (disability compensation, health care, education) with an official way to apply. Includes how the learner will protect the start date or which form they will use. GI Bill plan No program or school named, if the learner will use the GI Bill. The program, the school or training, and what is needed for it. Two options compared in the GI Bill Comparison Tool. Free accredited help No representative, or a paid company that is not accredited. The name and contact details of a VA-accredited representative or VSO from VA's search tool. The learner has contacted them or booked an appointment. Claim shark warning signs Fewer than three warning signs. Three warning signs of someone who should not be paid to file. The learner explains when an accredited attorney or claims agent may charge. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Who does VA accredit to help with claims?
options: Any company that advertises to veterans
VSO representatives, attorneys and claims agents
check.why: VA accredits VSO representatives, attorneys and claims agents.

check.q: A helper says they will file your first claim fast if you share your va.gov sign-in. What do you do?
options: Refuse, and find a free accredited representative with VA's search tool
check.why: Never share your sign-in; free accredited help is available through VA's search tool.
